claims.text: Thermomechanical processing can induce discrete, coherent, ordered B2 nanoprecipitates within a continuous disordered BCC matrix in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The proposed B2 nanoprecipitates can be made stepwise-controllable in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
A continuous BCC matrix containing discrete B2 precipitates can improve room-temperature ductility while maintaining high yield strength.
SCCPs can overcome the strength-ductility trade-off at ambient temperature.
The starting Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is nominally equiatomic or near-equiatomic.
The starting Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy can be a single-phase disordered BCC solid solution or a coarse BCC-B2 mixture with a continuous B2 matrix.
The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has a density of approximately 10-11 g/cm³.
RHEAs with a continuous ordered B2 matrix generally have high yield strength but poor room-temperature ductility.
Poor ductility in two-phase B2+BCC RHEAs is attributable to the ordered B2 phase forming the continuous matrix.
Aging or annealing between 800°C and 1200°C, with controlled cooling, provides a suitable processing window for forming the proposed microstructure.
Coherent SCCP interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission and relieve stress concentrations that cause premature crack initiation.
Keeping B2 precipitates discrete rather than continuous prevents a brittle network and enhances ductility.
Coherent ordered B2 precipitates provide precipitation strengthening sufficient to maintain high yield strength.
The processed Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy will achieve yield strength above 1.0 GPa and tensile ductility above 10% at room temperature.
The processed Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy can have a density below 10 g/cm³.
Conventional Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEAs with continuous B2 matrices or coarse precipitates typically have less than 5% room-temperature ductility.
W-based RHEAs have densities above 15 g/cm³.
The approach requires thermodynamic stabilization of discrete B2 precipitates without brittle intermetallic or amorphous phases and a processing window that preserves interface coherence.
Reducing the fractions of Hf and Ta, or replacing them with lighter elements, is necessary for a substantial density reduction.
The density reduction is bounded by the atomic weights of Hf, Mo, Ta, Ti, and Zr.

contradictions.description: The predicted density target is below 10 g/cm³, but density falsification occurs only above 11 g/cm³. An alloy with density from 10 to 11 g/cm³ would miss the stated target without falsifying the density claim.

The main hypothesis associates the nanoprecipitation intervention with reduced density, but the conditions and boundary statements attribute density reduction to changing heavy-element fractions. Thermomechanical precipitation control alone does not provide the stated density-reduction pathway.
